abstract: A number of semi-aquatic insects rapidly move across the water surface using interfacial flight. In this locomotion strategy, flapping wings generate thrust above the air-water interface while surface tension supports their weight. This close proximity to the air-water interface alters aerodynamic force generation through ground effect, potentially enhancing horizontal propulsion. Here, we demonstrate that near-surface flapping enhances horizontal thrust by up to 17% at shallow stroke-plane inclinations. Using a beetle-inspired flapping-wing robot, we systematically vary wing-surface distance (D/c, where D is the minimum trailing-edge-to-surface clearance during flapping, normalised by chord length c) and stroke plane inclination {beta} at Reynolds numbers of order 103. Locomotion experiments show increased acceleration and higher terminal velocity near the surface (D/c < 1) at shallow stroke plane angles ({beta} = 30{degrees} and 45{degrees}), while direct wind-tunnel force measurements confirm increased aerodynamic thrust, distinguishing this enhancement from changes in water-related resistance. Particle image velocimetry further reveals that near-surface flapping alters passive wing motion and surrounding flow, producing stronger backward-directed flow after stroke reversal and earlier leading-edge vortex development during the initial upstroke. These findings establish a configuration-dependent aerodynamic benefit of near-surface flapping, providing insight into insect-scale interfacial flight and opportunities for enhancing propulsion in bio-inspired robotic systems.
